source_text: πάλιν πρὸς Κολοσσαεῖς καὶ πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἐπέστειλεν· «ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ἀοράτου». 16.29 καὶ ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ἰωάννην δὲ εὐαγγελίῳ ὁ υἱὸς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ οὐσίαν πατρικῷ χαρακτῆρι ἐσφραγίσθαι παριστῶν εἶπεν· «τοῦτον γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἐσφράγισεν ὁ θεός». 16.30 συνυφεστηκυίας δὲ δηλονότι τῆς σφραγίδος τῷ ἀρχετύπῳ καὶ ἰσοτύπου οὔσης, καὶ ἐν ἑαυτῇ δὲ δεικνυούσης τελείως καὶ ἀληθῶς τὴν πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ πνεύματος ἁγίου μονάδα τῆς φύσεως. ἡ γὰρ σφραγίς, ὡς καὶ ὁ χαρακτήρ, τὸ ὅμοιον καὶ ἀνόθευτον σημαίνει. 16.31 ἐπεὶ καιρὸς εἰπεῖν καὶ τὸν πατέρα μὴ ἀγενήτως καὶ ἀσυγκρίτως ἔχειν, εἴπερ ἐξεικονίζεται καὶ χαρακτηρίζεται ὑπὸ γενητοῦ καὶ ἀνομοίου. 16.32 Τὰ θεῖα ταῦτα καὶ ἑρμηνείας ἀνεπιδεᾶ λόγια μὴ συνέντες ὀρθῶς, διαστρέφοντες δὲ καὶ ἀνθρωπίνοις νοήμασι μαχόμενοι τοῖς τοῦ θεοῦ ῥήμασι φάσκουσιν· «ἄλλο θεὸς καὶ ἄλλο εἰκὼν θεοῦ, ὡς ἄλλο ἄνθρωπος καὶ ἄλλο εἰκὼν ἀνθρώ που.» 16.33 καὶ τρόπον τινὰ εἰκόνι ἀκινήτῳ τὸν ζῶντα καὶ ἐνεργὸν θεὸν λόγον ἀπεικάζουσιν. κατ' οὐσίαν δὲ καὶ κατὰ πάντα εἰκών ἐστιν ἀπλανεστάτη καὶ ἄναρχος τοῦ πατρός, καὶ οὐ κατὰ μορφὴν καὶ σχῆμα, ὡς ὁ πλαστουργηθεὶς ἢ γεγλυμμένος ἄπνους καὶ οὐκ αὐτοκίνητος ἀνδριάς, οὐδὲ κατὰ εἶδος καὶ χρῶμα, ὡς ἡ τεχνητὴ καὶ μιμητὴ ἄφωνος εἰκών. ταῦτα γὰρ οὐδὲ κατὰ φύσιν, οὐδὲ μὴν εἰς ὅλα τὰ ἄλλα ἐκφαίνουσιν τὸν πρωτότυπον. 16.34 καὶ υἱὸς μὲν γὰρ ἀνθρώπου εἰκὼν οὐσίας τοῦ ἑαυτοῦ πατρός ἐστιν· ἀλλὰ συμβαίνει παραλλάττειν ἡλικίαν ἢ εἶδος ἢ γνώμην ἢ δύναμιν ἢ ἀξίαν ἢ τὰ συναμφότερα ἢ καί τι ἕτερον. 16.35 ὁ δὲ θεὸς λόγος ἀπαραλλάκτως καὶ ἀπηκριβωμένως εἰς ὅλα τὴν ἁπλῆν καὶ ἀσύνθετον καὶ ἀποίκιλον πατρικὴν θεότητα φυσικῶς καὶ ἀνάρχως ἐξεικονίζει. 16.36 Οὐδὲ γὰρ νοεῖν ἐξόν, ὡς κατά τι θεοῦ εἰκὼν καὶ παρά τι παραλλάττει· 16.36 οὐδὲ μὴν γίνεται «ἀσυγκρίτου» εἰκών· οὐδὲ δύναται διὰ τοῦ ἀνομοίου ἢ μικροτέρου ἢ ὑπεξουσίου τὸ ἀληθὲς καὶ ἀρχέτυπον καὶ μεῖζον καὶ αὐτεξούσιον καὶ ἀσύγκριτον φαίνεσθαι· οὐδ' αὖ διὰ τοῦ κτίσματος ἡ φυσικὴ μορφὴ τοῦ κτίσαντος κατανοεῖσθαι. 16.37 Οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ ἄλλη φύσις τὴν ἑτέραν ἐν ἑαυτῇ ἐπιδείκνυσιν. 16.38 Ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ εὑρίσκεται ἀνυπόστατος γεγενῆσθαι, ὅτε αἱρετικοὶ τὸν χαρακτῆρα οὐ διδόασιν ἔχειν αὐτὸν τῆς ὑποστάσεως. 16.39 ἀλλ' οὐδὲ ὁ ἀόρατος καὶ ἀσύνθετος καὶ ἀσχημάτιστος θεὸς εἰκόνα ἔχει οἵαν ἐκεῖνοι ἐμφαίνουσι μιμητικήν. 16.40 Παραλύει δὲ τὰ ἐκείνων σαφῶς καὶ ἡ ἐπαγωγὴ ἔχουσα· «οὐχ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ». 16.41 περὶ δὲ φυσικῆς εἰκόνος ὑφηγεῖται καὶ Μωϋσῆς οὑτωσί· «ἐγέννησεν Ἀδὰμ τὸν Σὴθ κατὰ τὴν ἰδέαν αὐτοῦ». οὐκ ἦν δὲ ἑτεροούσιος ἀναγκαίως ὁ Σὴθ τῷ Ἀδάμ, καὶ ὅμως ἰδέαν τὴν εἰκόνα καὶ ὁμοίωσιν τῆς οὐσίας ἐκάλεσεν. 16.42 _̓Αλλὰ καὶ περὶ ἀνθρώπου, φησίν, γέγραπται, ὅτι ἐστίν «εἰκὼν καὶ δόξα θεοῦ». 16.43 ἀλλ' οὐδαμοῦ, ὦ οὗτοι, ἄνθρωπος ἢ ἄλλο ποίημα γέγραπται εἶναι «ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως». 16.44 ἄλλο δέ ἐστιν ἄνθρωπον εἰκόνα εἶναι θεοῦ, τουτέστιν τὸ τεχνηθὲν τοῦ τεχνησαμένου, ὡς δίφρος τοῦ τέκτονος Σολομὼν γὰρ λέγει· «ἀναλόγως τῶν κτισμάτων ὁ γενεσιουργὸς θεωρεῖται», καὶ ἄλλο ἐστὶν κατὰ τὸ σύμμορφον καὶ ταυτούσιον καὶ συνάναρχον ἀπαύγασμα εἶναι δόξης καὶ χαρακτῆρα ὑποστάσεως ἐνυπόστατον καὶ ἀψευδέστατον. 16.45 φησὶν γάρ· «ὁ ἑωρακὼς ἐμὲ ἑώρακε τὸν πατέρα». ὁ δὲ ἑωρακὼς ἄνθρωπον οὐχ ἑώρακεν τὸν θεόν, ὡς ὁ θεασάμενος τὸν δίφρον οὐχ ἑώρακε τὸν τέκτονα. 16.46 ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀνάγκη τοῦ μόνου ἀοράτου θεοῦ μόνην ἀόρατον εἶναι ἐκείνην τὴν εἰκόνα καὶ οὐ τὸν κατ' εἰκόνα ὁρατὸν ἄνθρωπον. 16.47 Οὔτε οὖν ἄλλῳ ὅμοιός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός: γράφει γάρ· «τίς ὁμοιωθήσεται τῷ κυρίῳ ἐν υἱοῖς θεοῦ;» οὔτε τῷ ἑαυτοῦ πατρὶ ἀνόμοιος· «ἐγὼ γάρ», φησίν, «καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν». 16.48 οἱ δὲ κτιστῆς εἰκόνος ἔννοιαν ἐπὶ αὐτοῦ 16 λαμβάνοντες, ἐξομοιοῦνται τῷ Ναβουχοδονόσωρ ποιητὴν ἄψυχον εἰκόνα προσκυνεῖσθαι τυπώσαντι. 16.49 Καὶ τὸν Ἀδὰμ δὲ διὰ τὴν παρακοὴν ἐκ τοῦ παραδείσου ὁ θεὸς δικαίως ἔρριψεν· 16.50 τὸν δὲ λῃστὴν καὶ σὺν αὐτῷ τὸν Ἀδὰμ καὶ τὸ κοινὸν ὅλον γένος ὁ υἱὸς εἰσήγαγεν, ὡς ἴσος πάντως τῇ θεότητι καὶ ἀγαθότητι καὶ δεσποτεία τῷ ῥίψαντι τυγχάνων. 16.51 Ποῦ δὲ ἐγράφη ὅτι «ἀσύγκριτος ὁ πατὴρ» πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ μονογενῆ ἢ ὅτι ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ καὶ τῶν πάντων δημιουργὸς καὶ κριτὴς κατὰ τὴν θεϊκὴν αὐτοῦ καὶ ὅλων ἐξῃρημένην ἄπειρον φύσιν «κτίσμα» ἐστίν; ἢ ὅλως ὅτι ποτὲ «οὐκ ἦν»; 16.52 ἢ ποῦ ἰδικῶς ἔφη ὁ πατήρ. «ἔκτισά μοι υἱόν» ἢ ὁ υἱός·
pass_a_gloss: [... and] again to the Colossians and to the Hebrews he wrote: 'who is image of the invisible God'. 16.29 And in the Gospel according to John the Son, presenting his own substance as having been sealed with the paternal stamp, said: 'for this one the Father sealed, God'. 16.30 The seal plainly subsisting together with the archetype and being of equal impress, and showing in itself perfectly and truly the oneness of nature of Father and Son and Holy Spirit. For the seal, as also the stamp, signifies the like and unadulterated. 16.31 Since [otherwise] it is time to say that the Father too is not ungeneratedly and incomparably, if indeed he is imaged and stamped by a generated and unlike thing. 16.32 These divine oracles, also not in need of interpretation, not having understood rightly, but twisting them and fighting with human notions against the words of God, they assert: 'God is one thing and image of God another, as man is one thing and image of man another'. 16.33 And in some way they liken the living and working God Word to a motionless image. But according to substance and according to all things he is the most unerring and beginningless image of the Father, and not according to form and figure, as the moulded or carved breathless and not self-moving statue, nor according to look and colour, as the artificial and imitative voiceless image. For these neither according to nature nor indeed into all the other things show forth the prototype. 16.34 For a son of a man indeed is image of the substance of his own father; but it happens [that he] differs in age or look or mind or power or rank or the two together or also something other. 16.35 But the God Word without variation and with exactness into all things images the simple and uncompounded and unvaried paternal Godhead naturally and without beginning. 16.36 For it is not even permitted to think that in some respect he is image of God and in some respect varies. 16.36 Nor indeed does an image of an 'incomparable' come to be; nor can through the unlike or smaller or under-authority the true and archetypal and greater and self-authoritative and incomparable appear; nor again through the creature the natural form of the one who created be perceived. 16.37 For neither does another nature show forth the other in itself. 16.38 But also the Father is found to have become without hypostasis, when heretics do not grant him to have the stamp of the hypostasis. 16.39 But neither does the invisible and uncompounded and figureless God have an image such as those ones display, imitative. 16.40 And the continuation also clearly undoes their things, having: 'he did not consider a seizure the being equal to God'. 16.41 And about a natural image Moses too explains thus: 'Adam begot Seth according to his form'. And Seth was not necessarily of another substance than Adam, and nevertheless he called the image and likeness of the substance 'form'. 16.42 But also about man, he says, it has been written that he is 'image and glory of God'. 16.43 But nowhere, O you, has man or another made thing been written to be 'radiance of the glory of God and stamp of the hypostasis'. 16.44 And it is one thing for man to be image of God, that is, the crafted [image] of the one who crafted, as a stool of the carpenter: for Solomon says: 'analogously from the creatures the originator is beheld', and it is another thing according to the same-formed and same-substanced and co-beginningless to be radiance of glory and stamp of hypostasis, subsisting and most unlying. 16.45 For he says: 'the one who has seen me has seen the Father'. But the one who has seen a man has not seen God, as the one who has gazed at the stool has not seen the carpenter. 16.46 But also [it is] necessity that of the only invisible God only that image be invisible and not the visible man according to image. 16.47 Neither then is the Son like to another: for it writes: 'who will be likened to the Lord among sons of God?' nor unlike to his own Father: 'for I,' he says, 'and the Father are one'. 16.48 And those taking the notion of a created image upon him are made like to Nebuchadnezzar, who decreed that a made soulless image be worshipped. 16.49 And Adam too God justly threw out of the paradise on account of the disobedience; 16.50 but the robber and with him Adam and the whole common race the Son brought in, as being altogether equal in Godhead and goodness and mastership to the one who threw [him] out. 16.51 And where was it written that 'incomparable [is] the Father' toward his own only-begotten, or that his Son, also the craftsman and judge of all things, according to his divine and infinite nature set apart from all things, is a 'creature'? or at all that once 'he was not'? 16.52 or where did the Father say specifically: 'I created for myself a Son', or the Son: [...]
pass_b_english: … again he wrote to the Colossians and to the Hebrews: “who is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). And in the Gospel according to John, the Son, showing that his own substance has been sealed with the Father’s stamp, said: “For on him the Father, God, has set his seal” (John 6:27).

The seal, plainly, subsists together with the archetype and bears the same impress, and in itself shows perfectly and truly the oneness of nature of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For the seal, like the stamp, signifies what is like and genuine. Otherwise it would be time to say that the Father too is not ungenerated and incomparable, if he is imaged and stamped by something generated and unlike.

These divine oracles, which need no interpreter, they did not rightly understand. Twisting them, and fighting the words of God with human notions, they assert: “God is one thing and the image of God another, as a man is one thing and the image of a man another.” And in a way they liken the living and active God the Word to a motionless image. But he is the image of the Father in substance and in every respect, most exact and without beginning: not by shape and figure, like a statue moulded or carved, without breath and unable to move itself, nor by appearance and colour, like the image made by art, imitative and voiceless. For these show forth the prototype neither by nature nor indeed in all its other features.

A son of a man is indeed an image of the substance of his own father; but he may differ in age, or appearance, or disposition, or power, or rank, or in a combination of these, or in something else. But God the Word, without variation and with exactness in every respect, images the simple, uncompounded and unvaried Godhead of the Father, by nature and without beginning.

For it is not even permitted to think that he is the image of God in one respect and differs from him in another. Nor indeed can there be an image of the ‘incomparable’; nor can the true, the archetypal, the greater, the self-determining and the incomparable appear through what is unlike, or smaller, or under another’s authority; nor again can the natural form of the Creator be perceived through a creature. For no nature shows another nature in itself.

But the Father too turns out to be without hypostasis, when heretics will not grant that he has the stamp of his hypostasis. Nor does the invisible, uncompounded God, who has no figure, have an image of the imitative kind they present. And the words that follow plainly undo their views, for they run: “He did not count being equal to God a thing to be seized” (Philippians 2:6).

Moses too explains a natural image, in these words: “Adam begot Seth according to his form” (Genesis 5:3). Now Seth was of necessity not of a different substance from Adam; and yet Moses gave the name ‘form’ to this image and likeness of substance.

“But of man too,” he says, “it is written that he is ‘the image and glory of God’” (1 Corinthians 11:7). But nowhere, you people, is man or any other thing made written to be “the radiance of the glory of God and the stamp of his hypostasis” (Hebrews 1:3). It is one thing for man to be the image of God, that is, as the thing crafted is the image of its craftsman, as a stool is of the carpenter (for Solomon says: “By analogy from created things their Maker is beheld”); and it is another thing to be, in sameness of form, identity of substance and equal beginninglessness, the radiance of glory and the stamp of the hypostasis, having its own subsistence and wholly true.

For he says: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). But he who has seen a man has not seen God, as one who has looked at the stool has not seen the carpenter. Indeed, it is necessary that the image of the only invisible God be alone invisible, and not man, who is visible and made after the image.

So the Son is neither like another, for it is written: “Who will be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?” (Psalm 89:6); nor unlike his own Father: “For I and the Father,” he says, “are one” (John 10:30). Those who apply to him the notion of a created image become like Nebuchadnezzar, who ordained that a manufactured, lifeless image be worshipped (Daniel 3:1-6).

God justly cast Adam out of paradise for his disobedience (Genesis 3:23-24); but the Son brought in the thief (Luke 23:43), and with him Adam and the whole common race, since he is altogether equal in Godhead, goodness and lordship to him who cast Adam out.

Where is it written that “the Father is incomparable” with his own Only-begotten, or that his Son, the Maker and Judge of all, is a “creature” in his divine nature, infinite and exalted above all things? Or at all that once “he was not”? Or where did the Father say expressly, “I created for myself a Son”? Or the Son: …

lemmas.gloss: what is brought on next, continuation

choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English turned 16.31 (otherwise the Father too would not be ungenerated and incomparable) into 'it is not improper or incomparable to have the Father [as the archetype]', made 'these divine things' the subject of 16.32, read ἄναρχος (without beginning) as 'sovereign' (16.33, 16.35), ἀποίκιλον (unvaried) as 'unlike', ἀσύνθετον as 'undivided', ἐπαγωγή (the continuation of Philippians 2:6) as 'induction', split 16.38 into a stray sentence 'Not of his hypostasis.', called Seth's ἰδέα (Genesis 5:3) an 'idea' (reader report: Genesis SOURCE_ISSUES item 26), turned Solomon's saying (Wisdom 13:5) into one 'concerning the product of a carpenter', made Nebuchadnezzar worship an image 'made by [someone]', and rendered ἔκτισά μοι υἱόν (I created for myself a Son) as 'Create a son for me'. References: '(John 1:1)' after 'he was not' removed (the Arian slogan is not John 1:1); '(Col 1:15)' and '(Gen 5:3)' written in full; John 6:27 kept; Philippians 2:6, 1 Corinthians 11:7, Hebrews 1:3, Daniel 3:1-6, Genesis 3:23-24 and Luke 23:43 added; Wisdom of Solomon 13:5 recorded as a clear deuterocanonical reference. Bracket fillers '[as the archetype]', '[ones]', '[someone]', '[them]', '[say]' removed.

choices.term: πάλιν πρὸς Κολοσσαεῖς καὶ πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἐπέστειλεν
choices.english: … again he wrote to the Colossians and to the Hebrews
choices.why: The section opens after the καί that ends the previous section; a leading ellipsis marks the join. Only Colossians 1:15 has these words; Didymus pairs it with Hebrews 1:3, just quoted (see problems).

choices.term: τοῦτον γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ ἐσφράγισεν ὁ θεός
choices.english: For on him the Father, God, has set his seal
choices.why: Didymus' word order puts 'God' in apposition to 'the Father'; kept.

choices.english: Otherwise it would be time to say
choices.why: ἐπεί here introduces the absurd consequence of denying that the seal is like the archetype.
Single-nu forms (γενητός, having come to be); the pair keeps Didymus' play.

choices.term: κατὰ μορφὴν καὶ σχῆμα … κατὰ εἶδος καὶ χρῶμα
choices.english: by shape and figure … by appearance and colour
choices.why: The first pair is a statue, the second a painting (ἡ τεχνητὴ καὶ μιμητὴ ἄφωνος εἰκών). 'Shape' for μορφή here keeps 'form' free for ἰδέα in 16.41.

choices.english: or in a combination of these
choices.why: 'Both together': any two of the listed differences at once.

choices.term: ὅτε αἱρετικοὶ τὸν χαρακτῆρα οὐ διδόασιν ἔχειν αὐτὸν τῆς ὑποστάσεως
choices.english: when heretics will not grant that he has the stamp of his hypostasis
choices.why: The pronoun is ambiguous in the Greek (the Father having a stamp of his hypostasis, or the Son being it); the English keeps 'he' and lets the argument carry it: with no stamp, no hypostasis.

choices.english: the words that follow … for they run
choices.why: ἐπαγωγή is the continuation: after 'being in the form of God' Paul adds 'he did not count being equal to God a thing to be seized', which undoes the heretics' 'image'.
LXX Genesis 5:3 κατὰ τὴν ἰδέαν αὐτοῦ: Seth's likeness to Adam. Didymus' point is that Moses gives this name to an image of the same substance. 'Idea' (the old draft) is a false friend.
Didymus' blunt address to his opponents.

choices.term: ὡς δίφρος τοῦ τέκτονος Σολομὼν γὰρ λέγει
choices.english: as a stool is of the carpenter (for Solomon says …)
choices.why: The copy-text has no stop before Σολομών; the quotation is set in parentheses because it supports the craftsman image.

choices.term: κατὰ τὸ σύμμορφον καὶ ταυτούσιον καὶ συνάναρχον
choices.english: in sameness of form, identity of substance and equal beginninglessness
choices.why: Three compound neuter adjectives used as nouns; each rendered as a quality.

choices.english: having its own subsistence and wholly true
choices.why: ἐνυπόστατος: really subsisting, not a lifeless likeness; ἀψευδέστατος: most free of falsehood.

choices.english: who ordained that a manufactured, lifeless image be worshipped
choices.why: ποιητήν is the adjective 'made'; τυπόω in later Greek 'decree'. The old draft's 'worshipping an unconscious image' missed both.

choices.english: I created for myself a Son
choices.why: Aorist indicative, not an imperative; the Arian proof-text would need such a saying.
Printed line number 16 inside the Greek is page debris and is skipped.
Word split by a line break, and a stray underscore before ̓Αλλά, in the copy-text.
